summary: Year 5 pupils measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes (straight sides, with every corner made by sides meeting at right angles — rectangles joined, e.g. an L-shape). The distinctive skill is DEDUCING unmarked side lengths from the labelled ones: in each direction, the side lengths on one side of the shape add up to the side lengths on the opposite side. In an L-shape this means the two shorter sides along one direction add up to the opposite longer side (so a missing length is found by adding the two shorter sides, or by subtracting a known shorter side from the longer one); other shapes, such as U- or T-shapes, may have more than two parts on one side. Pupils then total every boundary side exactly once. Chief hazards: adding only the given numbers (forgetting missing sides), working out a missing length wrongly, including internal split-lines, double-counting a side, and confusing perimeter (a length in cm or m) with area (cm2 or m2).
misconceptions: Forgets to find the unmarked sides and adds only the given numbers.
Cannot see that the two shorter sides equal the opposite longer side, so mis-deduces a missing length.
Includes internal lines, double-counts a side, or confuses perimeter with area.

activities.title: Trace-the-boundary L-shape with live missing-side reveal
steps: Trace a finger (or pen) all the way around the boundary of an L-shaped figure, naming or ticking each side as you pass it so no side is counted twice and none is missed.

When you reach an unmarked side, work out its length from the labelled sides: the two shorter sides along a direction add up to the opposite longer side, so find a missing longer side by adding the two shorters, or find a missing shorter side by subtracting the known shorter length from the longer. Write the deduced length on the blank.
Keep a running total as you go; when every side is ticked, read off the perimeter in cm.
Notice the internal 'fold' line where the rectangles join: leave it out — it is not part of the boundary.
activities.insight: A hidden side length is not missing information: it can be recovered from the labelled sides, because the shorter sides along a direction add up to the opposite longer side. Perimeter is the total distance around the boundary, each side counted exactly once, excluding internal lines.

activities.title: Find-the-missing-side, total, and spot-the-mistake
steps: Given an L-shape with some sides labelled and some blank, find each unmarked side by adding or subtracting the labelled lengths along that direction, then total the whole perimeter.

Examine a worked solution where a character has made an error — e.g. included an internal join-line, or omitted an unmarked side — and say exactly which side is wrong and what the correct total should be.
Decompose the shape into rectangles to see why the two shorter sides add up to the opposite longer side.
activities.insight: The method has two stages — deduce all unknown sides, then add every boundary side once — and the common errors (adding only given numbers, including inside lines, double-counting, giving area instead) are specific and checkable.

activities.title: Draw a composite shape to a target perimeter
steps: On cm paper, draw a composite rectilinear shape (rectangles joined, straight sides that always meet at right angles) whose perimeter is exactly 40 cm.
Label every side and check that the total length across the shape in each direction balances.
Add all the boundary sides to confirm the total is 40 cm, ticking each side once.
activities.insight: Constructing a shape to a given perimeter — not just reading one — requires the pupil to control which sides are boundary, how deduced sides relate, and to keep length (cm) distinct from area.

checkQuestion: Give the child an L-shaped figure on cm paper with only some sides labelled (e.g. an outer 8 cm and 6 cm, and a notch with two sides given but two sides left unmarked). Say: 'Find its perimeter.' Then WATCH whether they deduce the unmarked sides from the labelled ones, whether they add every boundary side exactly once (and not the internal line), and whether they confuse it with area.
checkAnswer: Deduces the two unmarked sides from the labelled ones (opposite sides of the whole are equal, found by adding or subtracting known lengths), adds all boundary sides exactly once, and gives the perimeter in cm.
